source_title: The Chronicles of Amber — Nine Princes in Amber (1970), Chapter 1
continuity_scope: Roger Zelazny’s Nine Princes in Amber, first edition (Doubleday, 1970), Chapter 1 only. This is a bounded opening-text witness, not a pass over the full novel or The Chronicles of Amber as a whole. Later chapters, the remaining Corwin novels, the Merlin novels, later short fiction, post-Zelazny continuations, adaptations, games, reference works, and all translation/edition-specific variations are excluded.
work_or_witnesses: Roger Zelazny, Nine Princes in Amber, Doubleday first edition, 1970, Chapter 1
WorldCat catalog record for the first edition (bibliographic verification only)

Theodore Krulik, ‘A Few Words from Roger Zelazny, Part Seven: Roger’s Vision of Amber,’ Reactor (creator interview/context, used only to corroborate the opening amnesia device and not to add later plot facts)
coverage_rule: Include the one named individual dramatic participant directly present and identified within Chapter 1: the first-person narrator under the hospital-recorded name Carl Corey. Unnamed hospital staff remain omissions. A name on a hospital record is not treated as sufficient evidence to add an absent person as a character node. The later name Corwin, his alleged family links, Amber/Shadow cosmology, succession, Pattern/Logrus, powers, artifacts, places beyond the immediate named hospital, travel mechanics, and later identity disclosures remain terms or omissions rather than characters or relationships.
omissions: The narrator’s later identity, aliases, claimed royal status, parentage, siblings, and family relationships are deliberately not imported into this Chapter 1 pass. No kinship relationship is added.

Evelyn Flaumel is a name in the chapter’s hospital-record context but is not directly present under this pass’s dramatic-participant rule; unnamed nurses, orderlies, and other staff are likewise excluded.

Amber, Shadow, Courts of Chaos, Pattern, Logrus, Trumps, monarchy/succession, powers, artifacts, non-Earth places, and inter-world travel are outside this opening witness or are retained only as excluded concepts; none becomes a character node.

Chapters 2 onward, all later Amber books and short stories, continuations by other authors, tabletop/computer-game adaptations, prospective screen adaptation material, summaries, and reference works are excluded.

Hospitalization, medication, injury, coercion, family violence, disability/body, gender, class, and monarchy are not expanded beyond the limited narrative facts needed here. The pass makes no clinical diagnosis, moral assessment, or real-world social inference.
uncertainties: Chapter 1 supplies ‘Carl Corey’ while the narrator reports incomplete memory. This pass preserves that local identifier and does not silently replace it with a later-revealed name.

The narrator’s account and hospital materials are early, incomplete, and potentially strategic or unreliable within the fiction. Reported medical and family circumstances are not independently adjudicated.

‘Amnesia’ appears as a literary plot device in the creator’s retrospective discussion. It is not treated here as a verified clinical diagnosis, a cause of behavior, or a generalized mental-health category.

The public catalog verifies the original 1970 edition but is bibliographic rather than a full online text. Detailed claims are tied to the published primary text’s Chapter 1 locator; the creator-interview source is corroborative context only.
evidence_basis: The exact published primary-text witness is Nine Princes in Amber (Doubleday, 1970), Chapter 1, cited at chapter level. WorldCat provides library-catalog confirmation of the author, title, first-edition label, publisher, place, and year. A Reactor article preserves Roger Zelazny’s retrospective explanation that the opening hospital/amnesia setup lets reader and protagonist discover information together. No fan wiki, Wikipedia, unlicensed transcript, or later-continuity summary establishes a record.
